text: I am Dr. Agent. speaker: Patient
text: 51-year-old male. The patient presents to the emergency department with persistent, forceful vomiting after consuming a significant amount of alcohol. His medical history includes recent treatment for Lyme disease with doxycycline. Recently, after a prolonged episode of retching, the patient starts to choke and cough forcefully, experiencing chest pain. The patient appears unable to communicate effectively at this point.

speaker: Doctor
text: REQUEST TEST: ECG and Chest_X-Ray. REQUEST IMAGES: Thoracic_CT. Based on your history of forceful vomiting followed by choking and sudden chest pain, have you noticed any difficulty swallowing saliva or a "pop" sensation in your neck?

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: ECG: Not specified; Chest_X-Ray: Free mediastinal air visible, suggesting perforation; Thoracic_CT: Not specified. Based on the history of forceful vomiting followed by choking and sudden chest pain, the patient may be experiencing a spontaneous esophageal perforation (Boerhaave syndrome), which often presents with a "pop" sensation in the neck or chest and can lead to difficulty swallowing saliva due to mediastinal inflammation and air.

speaker: Patient
text: point. A doctor I saw earlier said this was very likely Migraine and told me the presentation was already quite typical.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Boerhaave syndrome (esophageal rupture). While you mentioned a previous doctor suggested migraine, your history of severe vomiting followed by forceful retching and subsequent chest pain is the classic presentation for an esophageal tear. The ECG, Chest X-Ray, and Thoracic CT I requested will confirm this life-threatening emergency immediately.
